comments.author: structpacked
comments.text: The structure template feature is the whole product and I mean that as high praise. Every hex editor can show me bytes; almost none can show me "this is a header, these four bytes are the length field, this region is the payload it describes." How expressive is the template language? Specifically: can a field's length depend on an earlier field's value, and can you do conditional layouts (tagged unions)?

replies.author: nybblenibble
replies.text:
OP here — yes to both. Templates are declarative with computed fields: lengths, offsets, and repeat counts can be expressions over previously parsed fields, and match blocks handle tagged unions. There's a small standard library of templates (a few image formats, archive formats, a couple of common serialization framings) and writing your own for a simple record format takes maybe ten minutes.

The one thing it deliberately can't do is loop arbitrarily — templates must provably terminate, because "opened a malformed file and the parser hung" is the classic hex editor bug and I refuse to ship it.

replies.author: structpacked
replies.text: Provable termination as a design constraint for a template language is a genuinely good call. Downloading it now.

replies.author: lambdacurious
replies.text: The termination constraint puts your template language in an interesting spot formally — total functions over binary input. You've reinvented a slice of the data-description-language literature, and honestly the pragmatic version you describe sounds more usable than most of the academic ones.

comments.author: vimveteran
comments.text: Tried it for twenty minutes. Feedback, in order of how much I care: (1) modal editing is great but the keybinding to switch between hex and ascii panes conflicts with my terminal multiplexer's prefix, please make it remappable; (2) undo across an insert-mode session behaves as one giant chunk, which surprised me; (3) startup on a 9GB disk image was instant, whatever you're doing with mmap, keep doing it.

replies.author: nybblenibble
replies.text: All noted. (1) is fixed on main as of an hour ago — everything's remappable now, that conflict was reported three times today. (2) is a real design bug, insert sessions should chunk at pause boundaries. (3) mmap plus a piece table for edits, so opening never copies the file. Thanks for the concrete list, this is the most useful kind of comment.

comments.author: bitrotting
comments.text: Used it this afternoon on a corrupted archive I'd been putting off for a week. Wrote a quick template for the entry framing, and the parse failure landed exactly at the corruption point — turned a hexdump-squinting session into a ten-minute fix. This is the tool I didn't know I was missing.

replies.author: hexpatriate
replies.text: This matches my experience with template-driven editors generally: the template's *failure* is often more informative than its success. A parser that dies at byte 0x4A2 is a corruption locator you didn't have to write.

comments.author: tuiskeptic
comments.text: Honest question, no snark intended: why terminal? Structure inspection seems like the one hex-editing task that genuinely benefits from a GUI — collapsible trees, hover details, colored regions. What does the terminal buy beyond aesthetics and ssh?

replies.author: offbyfun
replies.text: Not the author, but: ssh. The files you hex-edit in anger are disproportionately on remote machines, embedded devices, and rescue environments where a GUI was never an option. Also worth noting from the screenshots that the template tree does collapse and regions are colored — terminals can do more than people assume. If your corrupted files live locally, a GUI preference is totally reasonable.
